To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the X-ray flash XRT060218/SN 2006aj was a low-luminosity version of the class of GRBs/XRFs that includes the nearby GRB 980425/SN 1998bw, that it is a hundred times lower in luminosity than cosmological GRB/XRFs and ten times more common, and that it is distinguished from normal type Ibc supernove by the presence of relativistic ejectas.
XRF 060219 is the second nearest GRB, that it has an energy of 1046 erg, that this is 104 times less than the average cosmological GRB, and that it has a rate of 104 times the cosmological GRB rate.
the GRB XRF 060219 was a hundred times less powerful than typical GRBs but ten times more frequent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origin of relativistic outflows in the universe.
the origin of cosmic explosions.
the physics of GRB/XRF explosions and their central engines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the production of mildly relativistic ejectas is the key physical difference between GRBs and X-ray flashes (or ordinary core-collapse supernovae).

the XRF 060219 event is a hundredth of the energy of the most energetic GRBs but is ten times more common, with a total energy output of ~1048 erg, a central engine, and a central engine that is a magnetar or black hole.
the relativistic ejecta are the key physical distinction, and the nature of the compact object is a secondary distinction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the central engine of XRF 06 218 is a rapidly rotating neutron star with a magnetic field strength of ~10 ^{14} Gauss.
the X-ray flash XFR 060218 is an ordinary type Ibc SN with a relativistic component, and the rate of such events is comparable to that of type Ibc SNe.
XRF 060219 is a low-luminosity version of GRB 030329, which is the closest cosmological GRB identified until 2006.
The main takeaway from our work is that

X-ray flashes are a hundred times more common than gamma-ray bursts and that they are associated with the deaths of massive stars that are a hundred times less massive than the stars that produce gamma-ray bursts.
the rate of XRFs is much higher than the rate of cosmological GRBs, which implies that GRBs may not be the dominant mechanism for the production of heavy elements in the universe.
GRBs and X-ray flashes are not exotic events, but rather a natural consequence of the death of massive, rapidly rotating stars.
